topic: Driving Safely: Vehicle Inspection & Basic Control
question: During an inspection, how much steering wheel free play is considered a defect that can make a vehicle hard to steer?
choice_a: More than 10 degrees (about 2 inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch steering wheel)
choice_c: Any movement at all, even 1 degree
choice_d: More than a full turn of the wheel
explanation: The manual lists steering wheel play of more than 10 degrees -- approximately 2 inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch steering wheel -- as a steering system defect that can make the vehicle hard to steer.
source_note: Section 2.1.3 - What to Look For, Steering System Defects

topic: Driving Safely: Vehicle Inspection & Basic Control
question: Why are exhaust system defects, such as loose or broken pipes, mufflers, or mounting brackets, especially dangerous?
choice_a: A broken exhaust system can let poison fumes into the cab or sleeper berth
choice_b: They only cause excess noise with no safety risk
choice_c: They reduce fuel economy but pose no danger to the driver
choice_d: They are a cosmetic issue only
explanation: A broken exhaust system can let poison fumes into the cab or sleeper berth, so drivers must look for loose, broken, or missing exhaust pipes, mufflers, tailpipes, mounting brackets, and leaks.
source_note: Section 2.1.3 - What to Look For, Exhaust System Defects

topic: Driving Safely: Vehicle Inspection & Basic Control
question: According to the manual, what is prohibited regarding tires on the front wheels of a bus?
choice_a: Re-grooved, recapped, or retreaded tires are prohibited on the front wheels of a bus
choice_b: Only new tires may ever be used anywhere on a bus
choice_c: Radial tires are prohibited on the front wheels of a bus
choice_d: Bias-ply tires are prohibited on the front wheels of a bus
explanation: The manual specifically states that re-grooved, recapped, or retreaded tires on the front wheels of a bus are prohibited.
source_note: Section 2.1.3 - What to Look For, Tire Problems

topic: Driving Safely: Vehicle Inspection & Basic Control
question: What does rust around a wheel's nuts most likely indicate, and what should a driver do after a tire has been changed?
choice_a: Rust around the nuts may mean they are loose, so tightness should be checked, and nuts should be re-checked a short while after a tire change
choice_b: Rust around wheel nuts is purely cosmetic and never needs checking
choice_c: Rust means the rim needs to be repainted only
choice_d: Rust indicates the tire pressure is too high
explanation: Rust streaks around wheel nuts may mean the nuts are loose, so a driver should check tightness; after a tire has been changed, the driver should stop a short while later and re-check the tightness of the nuts.
source_note: Section 2.1.3 - What to Look For, Wheel and Rim Problems

topic: Driving Safely: Vehicle Inspection & Basic Control
question: Regarding the vehicle inspection report, what must the motor carrier do, and when must the driver sign it?
choice_a: The motor carrier must repair any items in the report affecting safety and certify repairs were made or unnecessary; the driver signs only if defects were noted and certified as repaired or not needing repair
choice_b: The motor carrier is never required to act on the report
choice_c: The driver must sign the report every day regardless of whether any defects were found
choice_d: Only a state inspector, never the motor carrier, may act on the report
explanation: The motor carrier must repair any items in the report that affect safety and certify on the report that repairs were made or were unnecessary; the driver signs only if defects were noted and certified to be repaired or not needing repair.
source_note: Section 2.1.5 - Seven-step Inspection Method, Step 1: Vehicle Overview, Review Last Vehicle Inspection Report

topic: Driving Safely: Vehicle Inspection & Basic Control
question: If the drive wheels begin to spin because of poor traction (rain or snow) while accelerating, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Take your foot off the accelerator
choice_b: Apply more power to regain traction
choice_c: Shift immediately into the highest gear
explanation: When traction is poor, speed up very gradually; if the drive wheels begin to spin, take your foot off the accelerator, since too much power can cause the wheels to spin and lead to loss of control.

topic: Driving Safely: Vehicle Inspection & Basic Control
question: How should a driver hold the steering wheel, and why?
choice_a: Firmly with both hands on opposite sides of the wheel, because hitting a curb or pothole could otherwise pull the wheel from your hands
choice_b: Loosely with one hand so you can react quickly
choice_c: With both hands at the top of the wheel only
choice_d: It doesn't matter as long as you are alert
explanation: Hold the steering wheel firmly with both hands on opposite sides of the wheel; if you hit a curb or pothole, the wheel could pull away from your hands unless you have a firm hold.

topic: Driving Safely: Vehicle Inspection & Basic Control
question: In the basic procedure for shifting down (downshifting) a manual transmission, what do you do after releasing the clutch and before pushing the clutch back in to shift to the lower gear?
choice_a: Press the accelerator to increase engine and gear speed to the rpm required in the lower gear
choice_c: Shift directly to neutral and coast
choice_d: Release the accelerator completely and wait several seconds
explanation: The basic procedure for shifting down is: release accelerator, push in clutch, and shift to neutral; release clutch; press accelerator and increase engine and gear speed to the rpm required in the lower gear; push in clutch and shift to the lower gear; release clutch and press accelerator.
source_note: Section 2.3.1 - Manual Transmissions, Basic Procedures for Shifting Down

topic: Driving Safely: Vehicle Inspection & Basic Control
question: Besides before starting down a hill, what is the other special condition listed in the manual where a driver should downshift before proceeding?
choice_a: Before entering a curve, so you can use some power through the curve for stability and speed up as you exit
choice_c: Before crossing a railroad track at any speed
explanation: The manual lists two special conditions for downshifting: before starting down a hill, and before entering a curve -- slowing down and downshifting before the curve lets you use some power through the curve for stability and to speed up once out of it.
source_note: Section 2.3.1 - Manual Transmissions, Before Entering a Curve

topic: Driving Safely: Vehicle Inspection & Basic Control
question: For a vehicle with an automatic transmission, why would a driver select a low range when going down a grade?
choice_a: To get greater engine braking, since the lower range prevents the transmission from shifting up beyond the selected gear (unless governor rpm is exceeded)
choice_b: To increase top speed on the downgrade
choice_c: Low range only affects air conditioning performance
choice_d: Automatic transmissions have no selectable ranges
explanation: With an automatic transmission, selecting a low range gives greater engine braking when going down grades; the lower range prevents the transmission from shifting up beyond the selected gear unless the governor rpm is exceeded, and it's important to use this braking effect on grades.
